questions.stem: A DynamoDB table uses an order status attribute, with values such as PENDING and SHIPPED, as its partition key. Most traffic goes to a few partitions and requests are throttled. What should the developer change?

options.text: Switch every read to strongly consistent
options.rationale: Consistency does not change how traffic is spread across partitions.

options.text: Use a high-cardinality attribute, such as order ID, as the partition key
options.rationale: Many distinct key values spread requests evenly across partitions.

options.text: Add a local secondary index that uses the status attribute as its sort key
options.rationale: An LSI shares the table's partition key, so the hot partitions remain.

options.text: Use Scan instead of Query to read orders
options.rationale: Scans read the whole table and use more capacity.

questions.explanation: A partition key with few values creates hot partitions; choose a key with many distinct values.

questions.stem: Right after updating an item in a DynamoDB table, an application reads the item back and sometimes gets the old value. The read must always return the latest data. What should the developer do?

options.text: Query a global secondary index with strongly consistent reads
options.rationale: Global secondary indexes support only eventually consistent reads.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table
options.rationale: DAX serves eventually consistent reads from its cache.

options.text: Set ConsistentRead to true on the GetItem request
options.rationale: A strongly consistent read reflects all writes that succeeded before the read.

options.text: Increase the table's read capacity
options.rationale: More capacity does not change the consistency model.

questions.explanation: Reads are eventually consistent by default; request a strongly consistent read when the latest value is required.

questions.stem: A DynamoDB table holds orders for many customers. An application must retrieve one customer's orders without reading the rest of the table. Which approaches will do this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Scan the table with a projection expression
options.rationale: A projection limits the attributes returned, not the items read.

options.text: Query a global secondary index keyed on customer ID
options.rationale: A GSI lets you query efficiently on an attribute that is not the table's key.

options.text: Run a parallel scan on the table
options.rationale: Parallel scans finish faster but still read the whole table.

options.text: Query the table when customer ID is its partition key
options.rationale: Query reads only the items with that partition key value.

options.text: Scan the table with a filter expression on customer ID
options.rationale: A scan reads every item; the filter only trims what is returned.

questions.explanation: Query reads by key; Scan reads everything. Design keys and indexes so access patterns use Query.

questions.stem: An existing DynamoDB table uses user ID as its partition key. The application now also needs to look up users by email address. What should the developer add?

options.text: A new local secondary index that uses email as its sort key
options.rationale: Local secondary indexes can only be created along with the table and keep the same partition key.

options.text: A filter expression on a Scan of the table
options.rationale: Scans read the whole table for every lookup.

options.text: A DynamoDB stream on the table
options.rationale: Streams record item changes; they do not enable new queries.

options.text: A global secondary index with email as its partition key
options.rationale: GSIs can be added to existing tables and use a different partition key.

questions.explanation: A new lookup key on an existing table calls for a global secondary index, which can be added later and has its own partition key. A local secondary index is the nearest distractor, but it can only be created with the table and keeps the table's partition key.

questions.stem: Session items in a DynamoDB table should be removed automatically a set time after they are created, without extra write costs. What should the developer use?

options.text: Time to Live (TTL), with an expiry timestamp attribute on each item
options.rationale: DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background without using write capacity.

options.text: A scheduled Lambda function that scans for and deletes expired items
options.rationale: This works but costs read and write capacity and needs code to maintain.

options.text: An Amazon S3 Lifecycle rule on the table
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules apply to S3 objects, not DynamoDB items.

options.text: A conditional write on each new item
options.rationale: Condition expressions control whether a write happens, not when an item expires.

questions.explanation: TTL takes an epoch timestamp attribute and removes items after that time.

questions.stem: Application logs are written to an Amazon S3 bucket. They must move to a cheaper archive storage class after 90 days and be deleted after one year. Which actions should the developer configure? (Select TWO.)

options.text: S3 Versioning on the bucket
options.rationale: Versioning keeps earlier versions; it does not move or delete objects by age.

options.text: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, with a retention period set to one year
options.rationale: Object Lock prevents deletion during retention and does not move objects to another storage class.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle expiration action at 365 days
options.rationale: Expiration actions make S3 delete objects once they reach a set age.

options.text: A DynamoDB TTL attribute on each log file
options.rationale: TTL applies to DynamoDB items, not S3 objects.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days
options.rationale: Transition actions move objects to another storage class once they reach a set age.

questions.explanation: One Lifecycle rule can hold a transition action (change storage class by age) and an expiration action (delete by age). Object Lock is the nearest distractor, but it prevents deletion and never moves objects.

questions.stem: An application stores user-uploaded videos that can be several gigabytes each. The data must be highly durable and served to users by URL. Which data store fits this access pattern?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
options.rationale: DynamoDB items have a small maximum size, so large files are usually kept in S3.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache
options.rationale: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, not durable storage for large files.

options.text: Amazon S3
options.rationale: S3 stores large objects durably and serves them over HTTPS.

options.text: Amazon RDS, with the videos in a binary column
options.rationale: Storing large binaries in a relational database is costly and slow to serve.

questions.explanation: Large objects go in S3; databases hold metadata and a pointer to the object.

questions.stem: A read-heavy application uses DynamoDB and needs microsecond read latency for repeated reads of the same items, with as few code changes as possible. Which caching solution fits?

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache with lazy loading code
options.rationale: This works but needs cache-management logic written into the application.

options.text: Amazon CloudFront in front of the table
options.rationale: CloudFront caches HTTP content at edge locations, not DynamoDB API calls.

options.text: An Amazon RDS read replica
options.rationale: Read replicas apply to relational databases, not DynamoDB.

options.text: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
options.rationale: DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that is API-compatible, so code changes are small.

questions.explanation: The clues are DynamoDB, microsecond repeated reads and few code changes: DAX is an API-compatible cache for DynamoDB. ElastiCache is the nearest distractor; it works, but the application must add its own cache-management code.

questions.stem: An application caches database query results in Amazon ElastiCache by using lazy loading. After records are updated, users sometimes see old data. Which changes will reduce stale reads? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Read from a database read replica instead of the primary
options.rationale: Replicas can lag, and the cache would still hold stale entries.

options.text: Set a time to live (TTL) on cached entries
options.rationale: Entries expire and are reloaded, which limits how long stale data can be served.

options.text: Use a larger cache node type
options.rationale: More memory holds more entries but does not make them fresher.

options.text: Turn off cache eviction
options.rationale: Keeping entries longer increases staleness.

options.text: Update or delete the cached entry on each write
options.rationale: Refreshing or removing the entry when the record changes keeps the cache in step with the database.

questions.explanation: Lazy loading only refreshes on a miss; add TTLs or write-through updates to limit stale data.

questions.stem: Logs in an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group grow without limit. The company needs only the last 30 days. What is the simplest way to keep only 30 days of logs?

options.text: Set the log group's retention period to 30 days
options.rationale: CloudWatch Logs deletes events older than the retention setting automatically.

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle rule for the log group
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules apply to S3 buckets, not log groups.

options.text: Write a scheduled function that deletes old log streams
options.rationale: This needs code and does not remove older events inside active streams.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB TTL attribute to each log event
options.rationale: TTL is a DynamoDB feature.

questions.explanation: Log groups keep data forever by default until you set a retention period.
